title: Seasonal campaigns without a new brand
metaTitle: Campaign pages inside the same brand
excerpt: A campaign page can be louder than the homepage and still use the same type, color, and offer. Give it a date, one action, and a plan for the day it ends.
alt: A two-lane road through red rock, with a single car far ahead and a mountain at the end, a louder stretch of the same route a campaign page should stay on.
caption: One road through red rock, and the same mountain. A campaign can be louder without a second brand. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Can a campaign page look different from the homepage?
faqs.answer: It can be louder. A bigger photograph, a plainer headline, and a date are fair. The type, the colors, and the offer should stay the ones the rest of the site already uses. A month does not need its own logo.

faqs.question: What should happen when the campaign ends?
faqs.answer: Decide before launch. Redirect the URL to the durable offer, or keep the URL and replace the hero, the title, and the date. Remove the campaign from the main navigation on the end date so the site does not advertise a closed moment.

faqs.question: What belongs in the browser title of a campaign page?
faqs.answer: A descriptive title that matches the visible heading, including the date when the date matters. Update it when you reuse the URL next year. A leftover title from last season is how a search result sends someone into a closed offer.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A campaign page can be louder than the homepage and still be the same company. Same type. Same colors. Same offer. Campaign landing page design is the work of turning the volume up inside that system, for a season, a launch, or a single audience, and then turning it back down.

Give the page an end. A month does not get its own brand. When the month ends, the page should be easy to retire without leaving a second visual language behind.

## What "louder" is allowed to mean

Louder means the visitor can tell, in one screen, that this is a specific moment. A seasonal line. A conference. A limited run. A price that is real for a window. The hero can be bigger. The photograph can be more specific. The headline can name the moment in plainer words than the homepage uses all year.

Louder does not mean a new logo, a new typeface, or a palette invented for the artwork. Those choices feel cheap to make and expensive to undo. The homepage, the product, and the receipt still have to look like one company on the morning the campaign ends.

Hanabi's public work is a useful check. Wabisabi holds a calm, tactile world. Ballarat Box Sports holds a community sports brand. A campaign for either would turn up a photograph, a date, and an offer. It would not repaint the identity for a holiday weekend. Thomas Bewick, the editorial heritage site, could run a seasonal essay or a print drop inside the same editorial system. The craft stays. The moment changes.

Write the campaign sentence before you art-direct it. Who it is for. What they can do until the date. What happens after the date. If that sentence only works in a display font nobody can read on a phone, the sentence is not done.

## Keep the offer the same offer

The homepage already says what you sell. The campaign page says why this week is a reason to act on that offer. If the campaign requires a different product, a different price logic, or a different customer, you are launching something else. Build that as its own page with its own name, and keep it inside the same type and color.

A founder often asks for a "microsite" because the artwork arrived from a printer or a sponsor. Artwork can fill the hero. The navigation, the button, and the sentence under the button should still match the rest of the site. A visitor who clicks through to shipping, sizing, or a demo should not feel they changed companies.

Down the Cove, an ecommerce migration and redesign, is a reminder that the shop and the story have to agree. A seasonal collection can have its own landing page. The cart, the product details, and the receipt stay on the store the customer already trusted. Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai are product interfaces with the same lesson on the software side: a campaign that drops someone into a product should land in the product they were promised, in the same voice.

Say the offer in the first screen in words, not only in the picture. Nielsen Norman Group notes that people often leave a page in 10 to 20 seconds, and that a clear value has to show up in about 10 seconds if you want them to stay. A beautiful crop with no sentence spends that window on mood. Mood can support the offer. It cannot replace it.

## Type, color, and the one accent

Start from the brand you already shipped. One type pair. The colors already in the system. Then decide the single accent the campaign is allowed to add.

An accent can be a photograph, a paper color, or one extra hue used on the campaign page and on the matching ad. It should not become a new primary button color across the site. Buttons are how people recognize an action. If the campaign button is a color the product never uses, the next click feels like a different tool.

Write the accent down. "This page may use the winter photograph and the existing red. It may not introduce a new green." Constraints like that keep a freelancer, an ad buyer, and a founder from each inventing a fourth color on a Friday.

Hanabi sets this in Figma before it is built, then ships it in the same front end as the rest of the site: Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, with Motion only where it helps the page and with a reduced-motion path. Illustrator is for the mark and the campaign art that must stay sharp. Framer is for a prototype when you need to feel the scroll before anyone writes production code. The campaign does not get a separate stack for a month.

Check the accent on a phone in daylight. Display type that looked sharp on a studio monitor often fails at the size a thumb actually sees. If the headline has to be two lines on a small screen, write a two-line headline. Do not ship a one-line poster and hope the browser will solve it.

## Titles, headings, and the date

The page needs one obvious title, and the title in the browser should describe this page. Google's guidance on title links asks for descriptive, concise text, and for a main heading that is clearly the main heading. It also warns that a title left over from last year can be wrong: if the visible page says this season and the title element still says last season, Google may use the visible text instead.

Put the date in the visible title when the date matters. "Spring delivery, orders through 12 April" is a title. "Campaign" is not. Update the title element when you reuse the URL next year. An obsolete title is how a search result sends someone into a closed offer.

Avoid a boilerplate title that every campaign shares, with only one word swapped. People, and Google, need to tell the pages apart. "Northwind: see the drop, the film, the makers, the stockists" repeated on six URLs tells nobody which page is which.

Keep the heading in the same language as the page. A campaign aimed at a local audience should not wear an English title on a page written in another language. Google's title guidance says the title should match the writing system of the primary content.

One H1. The importer of a blog is a separate problem. On your campaign page, the H1 is the offer for this moment. Subheads can name the date, the audience, and the limit. They should not compete at the same size.

## What the page must include

A stranger should be able to finish the job without hunting.

Name the thing. A product, a date, a city, a plan, a discount that is real. If the price is different for the window, show the price and the window together. A countdown with no offer is pressure without information.

Say who it is for, if that is narrower than the homepage. A wholesale window and a retail window are two pages, or two clear paths on one page. Mixing them in one hero makes both audiences wait.

Give one action. Buy, book, request the sample, register. Secondary links can sit under it: sizing, delivery, the ordinary product page for people who do not want the seasonal version. One action means one primary button.

Say what ends. The date, the quantity, or the cities. After that, say where the visitor goes when it is over. A page that 404s on the Monday after the launch trains people not to trust the next campaign. Redirect it to the durable offer, with a line that the seasonal page has closed.

Include the practical facts the offer depends on. Delivery cutoff. Whether the discount stacks. Who to write if the item is a gift. These lines are short. Leaving them off creates support mail, which is a worse design than a quiet list under the button.

## When the campaign ends

Decide the ending before you launch. Three clean options cover most cases.

Retire the URL with a redirect to the closest durable page, and keep the sentence in your archive if you need it for a report. Use this when the moment is over and the product remains.

Keep the URL and replace the hero with the ordinary offer, if the page has earned links you do not want to throw away. Change the title, the date, and the button. Google's title guidance treats a stale date as a defect. Update the visible heading and the title element together.

Leave a short record if the campaign was a public event people will search for later. A paragraph, the date, and a link to what exists now. This is an archive entry. It is not a second homepage.

Remove the campaign from the main navigation on the end date. A nav item called "Holiday" in March tells a new visitor the site is unattended. The footer can hold a quiet link for people who still have the old URL in a newsletter.

Store the art with the brand files. On a Hanabi project the client portal holds brand files, docs, and updates after delivery, so next year's campaign starts from the real logo and the real colors, not from a flattened poster someone found in a chat.

## A campaign is not a junk drawer of links

The page can point at a guide, a lookbook, or a short film. It should not become a list of everything you published this quarter. Each link has to help this visitor finish this offer.

If you are building a library of guides that outlive the season, give that library its own structure, grouped by the job a reader has. A reverse-chronological pile is an archive. The next piece, [a resources section that is not a blog dump](/blog/a-resources-section-that-is-not-a-blog-dump), is how to build that shelf so this campaign page can link to one useful guide instead of twelve.

If you want a second pair of eyes on a campaign that is starting to grow its own logo, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the homepage, the artwork, and the date the page should come down. The call should tell you what can get louder, and what has to stay.
